title: Valid Palindrome
summary: Check whether a string reads the same both ways after dropping non-alphanumeric characters and ignoring case. Put one pointer at each end, skip characters that don't count, compare, and move inward.

complexity.note: Best case is a mismatch on the first comparison. No cleaned copy of the string is built.

intuition: A palindrome mirrors around its centre, so compare `s[l]` with `s[r]` and move both inward.
Skip punctuation and spaces in place instead of building a filtered string.
Lower-case both characters before comparing.
Keep `l < r` in the inner skip loops so the pointers never cross.
pitfalls: Building a cleaned string uses O(n) extra space; the interviewer may ask for O(1).
Dropping the `l < r` guard in the skip loops runs off the end on strings like ".,".
`Character.isLetter` misses digits; the problem counts digits too.
input: s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"

title: Move Zeroes
summary: Move every zero to the end while keeping the order of the non-zero values, in place. A write pointer `w` marks where the next non-zero belongs; the read pointer swaps each non-zero into place.
intuition: Everything left of `w` is the non-zero values in their original order.
When `r` finds a non-zero, swap it to `w` and advance `w`.
Swapping (instead of overwriting) leaves the zeros behind at the end automatically.
pitfalls: Overwriting and then filling zeros works too, but takes two passes.
Moving zeros by shifting elements is O(n²).
Swapping when `w == r` is harmless; don't add special cases for it.

title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
summary: The array is sorted, so put one pointer at each end. If the sum is too small, move the left pointer right to increase it; if too big, move the right pointer left. The pointers meet the answer in one pass with O(1) space.

complexity.note: Best case is when the two ends are the answer.

intuition: Sorted order tells you which way to move: left increases the sum, right decreases it.
Moving the smaller side can never skip the answer, because that element can't pair with anything bigger than `r` either.
Return 1-based indices, as the problem asks.
pitfalls: Returning 0-based indices.
Using a hash map works but ignores the sorted property and the O(1) space requirement.
Binary search for each element is O(n log n).

title: Sort Colors
summary: Sort an array of 0s, 1s and 2s in one pass. Keep three regions: 0s before `lo`, 2s after `hi`, and 1s between `lo` and `mid`. `mid` scans the unknown region and swaps each value into its region.

complexity.note: Each element is examined once, in place.

intuition: Invariant: `[0, lo)` are 0s, `[lo, mid)` are 1s, `(hi, n)` are 2s, `[mid, hi]` is unknown.
A 0 swaps to `lo`; both `lo` and `mid` advance because the swapped-in value is a known 1.
A 2 swaps to `hi`; only `hi` moves, because the value swapped into `mid` hasn't been checked yet.
A 1 is already in place, so just advance `mid`.
pitfalls: Advancing `mid` after swapping with `hi` skips an unchecked value.
Looping `while (mid < hi)` misses the last element; it must be `mid <= hi`.
Counting sort is two passes; the follow-up asks for one.

title: 3Sum
summary: Find all unique triplets that sum to zero. Sort the array, fix the first number `nums[i]`, then solve Two Sum II on the rest with two pointers. Skip equal neighbours to avoid duplicate triplets.

complexity.note: Sorting is O(n log n); the pair search is O(n) for each i. Output space not counted.

intuition: After sorting, each fixed `nums[i]` turns the problem into finding a pair summing to `-nums[i]`.
Two pointers find that pair in O(n) because the array is sorted.
Skip `nums[i] == nums[i-1]` so each first value is used once.
After a hit, step both pointers past equal values so the same pair isn't added again.
If `nums[i] > 0`, nothing after it can sum to zero, so stop.
pitfalls: Using a HashSet of lists to dedupe is slower and still needs sorted triplets.
Skipping duplicates of `i` with `nums[i] == nums[i+1]` drops valid triplets like [-1, -1, 2].
Forgetting to move both pointers after a match causes an infinite loop.

title: Container With Most Water
summary: Pick two lines that hold the most water: area = min(height) × width. Start with the widest pair and always move the shorter line inward, since keeping it can never produce a bigger area.
intuition: The shorter line limits the area. Any container that keeps it and is narrower is strictly worse.
So moving the shorter pointer is the only move that might find a bigger area.
Track the best area seen along the way.
pitfalls: Moving the taller line can only lose area.
Checking every pair is O(n²) and times out.
Width is `r - l`, not `r - l + 1`.

Python.code:
def maxArea(height: List[int]) -> int:
    l, r, best = 0, len(height) - 1, 0
    while l < r:
        area = min(height[l], height[r]) * (r - l)
        best = max(best, area)
        if height[l] < height[r]: l += 1
        else: r -= 1
    return best

title: Trapping Rain Water
summary: Water above a bar is `min(maxLeft, maxRight) - height`. With two pointers, the side with the lower bar is limited by its own running max, because the other side is known to have something at least as tall. So process that side, add its water, and move inward.

complexity.note: One pass with four variables, instead of two O(n) max arrays.

intuition: Water at i is `min(leftMax, rightMax) - h[i]`.
If `h[l] < h[r]`, the right side has a bar ≥ h[l], so the water at l depends only on `leftMax`.
Update the running max first; if the current bar is the new max, it holds 0 water.
Move the pointer on the lower side and repeat until they meet.
pitfalls: Using the global max instead of the running max on each side.
Computing max arrays is fine (O(n) space) but know the O(1) version.
Moving the taller side gives wrong answers.
